questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Displacement of a Particle Given Its Velocity
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t$ is given by $v(t)=8{t}^{2}-3t.$ What is the total displacement of the particle between $t=0$ and $t=6?$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the total displacement by calculating the definite integral of the velocity.

Let $d$ be the total displacement. Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={\int }_{0}^{6}(8{t}^{2}-3t)\,\text{dt} \\  & ={(\frac{8{t}^{3}}{3}-\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2})|}_{0}^{6} \\  & =[\frac{8(6)^{3}}{3}-\frac{3(6)^{2}}{2}]-[\frac{8(0)^{3}}{3}-\frac{3(0)^{2}}{2}] \\  & =[576-54]-0 \\  & =522.\end{aligned}
$$

So the total displacement between $t=0$ and $t=6$ is $522.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem:
A particle $Q$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)={sec}^{2}⁡(t).$ At time $t=0$ the particle is located at the position $x=-2.$ 
Find the position of the particle at time $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Do not round the answer.

The position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is $x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is equal to its position at $t=0$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\frac{\pi }{4})=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-2+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2+{[\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-2+\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(0) \\  & =-2+1-0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is $x=-1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem:
A particle $Q$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{4}).$ At time $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ the particle is located at the position $x=1.$ 
Find the position of the particle at time $t=\pi .$ Do not round the answer.

The position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is $x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is equal to its position at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\pi ].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\pi )=x(\frac{\pi }{4})+{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\pi ) & =1+{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =1+{[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{4})]}_{\pi /4}^{\pi } \\  & =1+([-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi -\frac{\pi }{4})]-[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{4})]) \\  & =1+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =1+(-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})+1) \\  & =1+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1 \\  & =2+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is $x=2+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{6}).$ At time $t=0$ the particle is located at the position $x=3.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=\frac{\pi }{6}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is equal to its position at $t=0$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{6}].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\frac{\pi }{6})=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{7}{2}+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t \\  & =3+{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{6})]}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =3+([\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}-\frac{\pi }{6})]-[\operatorname{sin}⁡(0-\frac{\pi }{6})]) \\  & =3+(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{6})) \\  & =3+(0-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =3+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is $x=\frac{7}{2}.$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{3}).$ At time $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ the particle is located at the position $x=\frac{1}{2}.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=\pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is equal to its position at $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\pi ].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\pi )=x(\frac{\pi }{3})+{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{2}+{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+{[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{3})]}_{\pi /3}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+([-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi -\frac{\pi }{3})]-[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{3})]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+(-(-\frac{1}{2})+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is $x=2.$

questions.problem:
A particle $Q$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)={2}^{2t-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=-5.$ 
Find the position of the particle at time $t=3.$ Do not round the answer.

The position of the particle at $t=3$ is $x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=3$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,3].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(3)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{3}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(3) & =-5+{\int }_{1}^{3}({2}^{2t-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-5+{[{2}^{2t-2}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =-5+{2}^{2(3)-2}-{2}^{2(1)-2} \\  & =-5+{2}^{4}-{2}^{0} \\  & =-5+16-1 \\  & =-5+15 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=3$ is $x=10.$

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
x(9)=5+2=7.

canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t$ is given by $v(t) = 2t + 3t^2.$ What is the total displacement of the particle between $t=1$ and $t=3?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We find the total displacement by calculating the definite integral of the velocity.

Let $d$ be the total displacement. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(2t+3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={({t}^{2}+{t}^{3})|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =[{3}^{2}+{3}^{3}]-[{1}^{2}+{1}^{3}] \\  & =[9+27]-[1+1] \\  & =36-2 \\  & =34.\end{aligned}
$$

So the total displacement between $t=1$ and $t=3$ is $34.$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t) = 6t^2 +4t.$ At time $t=2$ the particle is located at the position $x=-20.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=4?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=4$ is equal to its position at $t=2$ plus the total displacement over $t\in[2,4].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(4) = x(2) + \int_2^4 v(t)\,\textrm{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(4) & =-20+{\int }_{2}^{4}(6{t}^{2}+4t)\,\text{dt} \\  & =-20+{[2{t}^{3}+2{t}^{2}]}_{2}^{4} \\  & =-20+([2(4)^{3}+2(4)^{2}]-[2(2)^{3}+2(2)^{2}]) \\  & =-20+([128+32]-[16+8]) \\  & =-20+(160-24) \\  & =-20+136 \\  & =116.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=4$ is $x=116.$
